Outbreak

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
17 cases of measles are confirmed in Gauteng, linked to a family who chose not to immunise their children. We analyse cracks in the country's voluntary vaccination programme that put us all at risk.

Unique Selling Point:
When Johann van den Heever, manager of South Africa's Extended Immunisation programme for 11 years resigned in protest over cracks in the programme early last year, the Department of Health slated him for speaking out about problems that he had said would make all South Africans vulnerable for diseases that should and could have been eradicated by now.

The departing manager was interviewed by Science Writer Chris Bateman who published the interview in the South African Medical Journal that showed how severe understaffing, vaccine stock-outs and poor follow-up was causing children not to get the full complement of shots they should. Bateman will speak to us about the facts uncovered by his story a year ago -- the former manager was lambasted and runs scared of speaking out again.

South Africa makes 11 antigens available in the extended immunisation schedule -- from measles, to the most recent HPV vaccine for protecting young girls agains caner of the cervix. Thanks to vaccines, polio and diptheria and whooping cough have been eliminated. But aside from measles, Kwazulu-Natal saw a resurgence of diptheria two years ago.

Through outbreak data and case studies we can basically track and confirm problems in the system as one outbreak after another hits the headlines -- there have now been three measles outbreaks (from over 31 confirmed cases in Stellenbosch to JHB) before the winter season, traditionally outbreak season, has even started.

Bateman warned in his article that missed vaccine doses were causing our herd immunity to be diminished, which would open doors to infections that could and should have been prevented.

Add to this the growing, if misguided fear that vaccines cause illness and autism in children, and the country's promise to the world community that we would eradicate measles by 2020, after the WHO DECADE OF VACCINES, seems highly improbable.

A massive educational responsibility rests on media in covering the outbreak -- the Lancet publication in 1998 by scientist Andrew Wakefield that linked the measles, mumps and vaccine to autism has been withdrawn, and described by Lancet as unethical, dishonest and fatally flawed. And yet this thinking continues to feed fears around autism.

The minister of health recently said members of the anti-vax lobby (resperented by VASA, Vaccine Awareness SA) are no better than bio-terrorists for placing everyone at risk by eroding the good work done by the department over many years. But it's not just those who CHOOSE not to vaccinate that cause the problem -- it's also those who forget, because their babies look well...and other migrants that fall out of the system, for a variety of logistical reasons -- shown in WHO studies in SA that we will review.


Summary:
Our proposal is to start with BATEMAN, to show the cracks in the immunisation programme -- then to look at the outbreak map that the National Institute of Communicable Diseases keeps (any instance of 3 laboratory-confirmed cases constitutes an outbreak).

We will tell of 2 TYPES OF PATIENTS/CASE STUDIES who fall through the cracks -- the anti-vax child whose parents object for factual or religious beliefs; as well as the child who misses a dose due to vaccine stockouts, poor follow-up or unavailability of staff.

We will show the history of some of the most dangerous illnesses successfully eradicated through vaccines and show the science "fixed" by Lancet after the damaging publication of the WAKEFIELD study in 1998. Turns out he wasn't interested in eradicating vaccines...but in replacing the vaccine in use with his own invention.




Further information:
STOCKOUT: VACCINES THAT DON’T ARRIVE
21 FEBRUARY, 2017 EUROSCIENTIST

Everyone agrees that these shortages are a global problem, due to the fact that the vaccines are developed by just a handful of companies, those with the sufficient human and financial capacity. If one of these companies has production problems, countries have few alternatives to satisfy demand. In cases of high demand, the market becomes saturated and the companies are unable to satisfy demand to all countries. Whilst certain, this excuse restricts liability to uncontrollable, external, factors. Internal factors are not curbed and are only reported by healthcare staff. On a global level, according to World Health Organization data (WHO), 97 countries accounted for that they were left without at least one of the essential vaccines in 2015 (the last year for which data is available) either on a national level on in certain areas. In Africa, 66% of countries acknowledged supply disruption. In America and Europe one in every two countries admitted having suffered this problem. Taking into account the fact that not all countries communicate this information to the WHO, the real number of countries without vaccines at any moment could be greater still.

Out of stock against tuberculosis. The anti-tuberculosis BCG vaccine is a prime case of a supply problem, caused by a production failures in one of the main labs of this vaccine, Statens Serum Institute, based in Denmark. Due to global shortages in 2015, 54 countries reported stock shortages this year. The majority of these countries are in Africa (21) and Europe (14). In 2015, UNICEF, who supply this vaccine to countries where tuberculosis is endemic, reported a global supply shortage of 16.5 million doses. Beyond the crisis that year, many countries have been lacking the BCG vaccine for over a decade.

Stockouts of anti tuberculosis vaccine. Number of years in the last decade which stockouts reported to the WHO in the last decade. Currently, stock problems with the tuberculosis vaccine persist, including in countries that had never previously reported a shortage of the antigen to the WHO, such as Spain, Australia and France. In the case of France, where the vaccine is no longer obligatory since 2007, Sanofi Pasteur (the French pharmaceutical company specialised in vaccines) diverted its stock which was destined for the Polish market in order to satisfy domestic demand. This diversion was introduced as an “interim measure” in March 2016.

In South Africa, this vaccine is especially relevant and its shortage is “a real problem”, according to Doctor Anban Pillay, Deputy Director of the Department of Health. Although its effectiveness is limited against pulmonary tuberculosis, its most common manifestation, the WHO recommends its administration to new born babies in countries where the incidence (morbility) of tuberculosis is high. In South Africa, morbility is huge: with 834 cases for every 100,000 people, the country has the highest rates of this disease, often compounded by the impact of HIV.

The BCG vaccine supply crisis is worsened by the concentration of production in few companies. And low profit margins makes it an unattractive venture for other laboratories which have the capacity to produce it, appoints Pillay. The oligopoly of the vaccines industry is even more concentrated: Sanofi Pasteur, Merck, Pfizer and GlaxoSmithKline take around 80% of the proceeds globally from the sales of these products.

Bexsero stockout in the EU - Bexsero, the only vaccine available in the European Union which protects against Meningitis B, the most common serogroup in the continent, is currently suffering distribution problems. The antigen, produced by GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) is approved in over 35 countries, between which are the EU member states, Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Canada, Brazil and the USA. This last country also depends on another drug for the disease, Trumemba. In Spain, where the vaccine is recommended but unsubsidised, pharmacies offer waiting lists of up to six months to obtain a dose (at a retail price of 105€). GSK Spain asserts that they will receive new doses in the second quarter of 2017. Other GSK subsidiaries have also reported problems with the manufacture of this vaccine, like in Australia and in the United Kingdom, due to “unanticipated global demand”.

Lack of control in South Africa - In South Africa, provinces that default on their payments for vaccines are another of the missing links in the supply chain, according to Shabir Madhi, director of the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD).

The South African government negotiates the prices and Biovac, a public-private partnership, receive the raw materials from the pharmacists. In their premises in Ciudad del Cabo, they fill vials and distribute the orders that they receive from provinces. Both Madhi and Pillay claim that Biovac has frozen supply to certain provinces which have not paid.

Once the vaccines have been distributed to the South African clinics the stock management problems begin to arise. Karl le Roux, doctor and researcher from Zithuele hospital, analysed the causes and effects of vaccines stockouts in the OR Tambo district, in the Eastern Cape province. According to his research, the shortages are due to a lack of space in the clinics, inadequate stock management systems, overworked staff and poorly trained nurses (that make orders for inadequate quantities), lack of responsibility in the provincial storage and theft.

Moreover, the state of the roads and the distance from storage facilities to healthcare centres are even more important in rural areas. Le Roux tells, for example, that there are 90 kilometres of very poor roads between Zithuele hospital and its medicine depot.

For this rural doctor “it is frustrating not being able to offer a patient what you know they need”. As soon as there is a shortage of vaccines, the centres are swamped as patients have to return. In his research, Karl le Roux shows that the lack of vaccines in clinics meant that 56% of children surveyed did not complete their courses of immunisation, according to their mothers.

Unreliable data - Johann Van der Heever, who managed the South African immunization programme for 11 years, blames the lack of control squarely on the Department of Health: “You have to staff adequately to the chain, you have to provide equip supervision and monitoring which is a function of the National Department”.

In an article in the South African Medical Journal magazine, which cites Van der Heever’s criticisms of the national immunization programme and condemns the government’s neglect of the situation, the national cold-chain manager (imperative system for the conservation of the antigens), admits that they were only able to inspect between 5% and 10% of facilities. Van der Heever regrets that, despite the fact that controlling the deterioration of vaccines was one of his priorities, the wastage is unknown, as it “requires very good supervision and support”.

“One of the big problems that we have is manufacturers have been aware that they have a shortage but they have not been willing to share that information, unlike in the United States or in Europe, where they are obliged by law”, alleged the Deputy Director of the Department of Health, Anban Pillay. Given the time required to produce each vaccine, both internal and external information is imperative in order to avoid stockouts. “You can only be foresighted if you have the information”, stated the healthcare manager.

The only way to approach to the real situation is through the Stop Stockouts Project (SSP), a platform that monitors the lack of medicines and vaccines in South Africa. Behind the project are organisations such as Médecins Sans Frontières, the Treatment Action Campaign and the Rural Health Advocacy Project, which created the campaign in light of the persistent lack of antiretroviral drugs in the country which has the highest number of HIV cases in the world (over 6.9 million people): one in five adults is seropositive.

At the end of each year, SSP conducts a telephone interview about vaccines and stockouts with over 2,400 of the 3,547 healthcare centres that they have identified across the country. Whilst Jacob Zuma’s government only reported its stock issues with the BCG vaccine to the WHO in 2015, Stop Stockouts recorded that 9% of healthcare centres contacted did not have the combined vaccine (composed of the DPT vaccine and the vaccines against Polio, Hib and Hepatitis B) available; 4% did not have the rotavirus vaccine available and 3% had a shortage of measles vaccines.

The data is indispensable: to control the existence of vaccines in stores, to know when to make an efficient order for a clinic and to design effective vaccination campaigns that avoid possible outbreaks in communities with low immunisation rates. Coordinated administration and the shouldering of responsibilities is vital to avoid shortages and stockouts of vaccines nationwide. But above all, South Africa cannot allow its people to lose faith in its healthcare system.

South Africa: managing in the dark - Problems with data in South Africa do not only affect stock levels; the most basic data, such as immunization rates, are not reliable. The lack of an up-to-date and detailed survey on vaccination coverage makes it impossible to control and avoid possible outbreaks, according to Shabir Madhi of the National Institute of Contagious Diseases in South Africa, as it is not known in which areas immunization is lower than recommended. “We do not know the actual coverage against measles,” laments Madhi. In addition, the WHO reduces by more than 20 points the levels of coverage that South Africa presents to them. Madhi, who estimates that the real figure must be between both values, urges to carry out a new survey to solve this situation.

Press Release:


Outbreak
First in Cape Town and now in Gauteng – scientists have confirmed over a hundred cases of highly contagious measles. South Africa’s voluntary childhood
vaccination programme was intended to prevent the mass outbreak of disease, but these cases are an indication that the system may be flawed. Are there
cracks in the country’s vaccination plans?



Script:


SCRIPT: Outbreak
TX DATE: TBC
PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg
PRESENTER: John Webb
The plan was to eliminate measles worldwide by 2020. But outbreaks are flaring up -- 6 600 cases in Romania; 2 800 in Italy; and in Minnesota, USA, 78 since April. Most had not been vaccinated against measles and one sick person can infect up to 15 others. In South Africa 83 cases were confirmed up to mid-June. One of the first was 17-year-old Neels Neethling from Paul Roos Gimnasium in Stellenbosch. (31 seconds)
References for numbers: Romania, Italy: http://ecdc.europa.eu/en/press/news/_layouts/forms/News_DispForm.aspx?ID=1631&List=8db7286c-fe2d-476c-9133-18ff4cb1b568&Source=http%3A%2F%2Fecdc%2Eeuropa%2Eeu%2Fen%2Fpress%2Fepidemiological_updates%2FPages%2Fepidemiological_updates%2Easpx / Minnesota: http://www.health.state.mn.us/divs/idepc/diseases/measles/#1
NEELS NEETHLING, MATRIC PUPIL: PAUL ROOS GIMNASIUM: My roommate said to me I must go away so that he doesn’t contract it, because it spreads quickly.
His mom, GP Amanda Neethling, was first to spot the telltale rash and made sure Neels got treatment quickly. (7 seconds)
AMANDA NEETHLING, MOM AND GENERAL PRACTITIONER: Within hours, your child just gets more ill and you get really nervous. I was also afraid, you know, there is a chance of a secondary infection. And then the fact that you know your child was immunised and you don’t quite understand why the child contracted it.
Paul Roos Gimnasium was on high alert. They considered it their legal and ethical duty to go to lock-down. Spokesman Neville Rothman. (8 seconds)
NEVILLE ROTHMAN, COMMUNICATION MANAGER: PAUL ROOS GIMNASIUM: Between Paul Roos, Bloemhof Girl’s School and Renish Girl’s School we had a collective meeting with the experts and they told us that containment was the most important...but they encouraged us to almost not get involved with other sporting activities...we do not want to be seen as compromising other people.
In the end, 7 pupils contracted measles. There’ve been 29 cases in the Western Cape. Before vaccines, millions - mostly kids under 5 - died of measles and thousands developed complications like blindness and pneumonia annually. Vaccines also prevent other deadly diseases like polio and diphtheria. (18 seconds) (source: http://www.nicd.ac.za/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/MeaslesGautengAlertJune2017.pdfhttp://www.nicd.ac.za/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/MeaslesGautengAlertJune2017.pdf)
(http://apps.who.int/iris/bitstream/10665/44855/1/9789241503396_eng.pdf)
(http://www.who.int/mediacentre/factsheets/fs286/en/)
JOHN LINK: Whenever cases of measles, diphtheria or meningitis in particular are identified, they tend to be referred to as outbreaks, but is that the result of an exaggeration by government or a valid reason for concern?
Prof Shabir Madhi, award-winning vaccine scientist who played a key role in developing the rotavirus and pneumococcal vaccines, heads the government-funded National Institute for Communicable Diseases that must confirm whether a sore throat and runny nose means measles. (16 seconds)
PROF. SHABIR MADHI, DIRECTOR: NATIONAL INSTITUTE FOR COMMUNICABLE DISEASES: When we see this sort of measles outbreaks, it’s a good indicator in terms of how well our immunisation program is working and the reason for that is unlike for many of the other diseases that we’ve vaccinate against, measles is the most contagious of all of them.
Last month, 17 cases were confirmed in Gauteng. Now, Azaadville on the West Rand is the hot spot, with 8 cases so far, mostly adults. (9 seconds)
PROF. SHABIR MADHI, DIRECTOR: NATIONAL INSTITUTE FOR COMMUNICABLE DISEASES: Right now we’re not actually at the peak of this epidemic. Right? If we’re not careful this figure of roughly about 85 cases that we’ve observed in Gauteng in the past two or three months, is going to be exactly what it was in 2009/2010 and that is going to 20 000 as a conservative estimate. And that’s when we see many more children dying. Right? So right now, this is… we’re sort of still brewing an epidemic.
Our Expanded Programme on Immunisation -- or EPI -- is run by the health department under the guidance of the World Health Organisation. Eleven vaccines are given without cost at clinics, but not every child gets it/them?. (13 seconds) (source: http://www.afro.who.int/en/south-africa/country-programmes/4245-expanded-program-on-immunization-epi.html)
JOHN LINK: A successful immunisation program could lead to healthier children and adults in the long run and help ease the burden on the public health system, but ironically the country’s vaccination program appears to become another victim of that self-same overburdened and understaffed system.
Prof Greg Hussey runs the National Advisory Group on Immunisation that works with the Minister and Department of Health to find and fix problems in the system. (9 seconds)
PROF. GREG HUSSEY, DIRECTOR: VACCINES FOR AFRICA: Our supply chain is not functioning optimally. Stockouts occur because of poor stock management firstly and secondly supply. The Minister in his budget speech alluded to the fact that they’re trying to rectify that. They now have electronic system to monitor stocks of all medication in clinics and hospitals. We’ve had major issues globally with supply of vaccines.
To begin to eliminate measles at least 95% of children must get both prescribed doses -- at 6 and 12 months old. (8 seconds)
NTOMBI MAZIBUKO, DIRECTOR: CHILD, YOUTH AND SCHOOL HEALTH, DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH: The health system as a whole there are quite a lot of challenges...it looks like an easy programme but the important thing is that caregivers, parents must still take their children to a health facility.
At the National Department of Health, Ntombi Mazibuko works on innovations in the hope it will get more kids covered. (6 seconds)
NTOMBI MAZIBUKO, DIRECTOR: CHILD, YOUTH AND SCHOOL HEALTH, DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH: We are now looking at making sure that people are empowered -- otherwise why will they go to the clinic and stand in the queue the whole day, for my child is not sick... The Minister launched what we call MOMCONNECT -- a service where mothers register when they’re pregnant.
The SMS service, which works on any phone, is meant to remind moms of vaccination dates...and to report problems at clinics. (7 seconds)
NTOMBI MAZIBUKO, DIRECTOR: CHILD, YOUTH AND SCHOOL HEALTH, DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH: The mothers can also through the MOMCONNECT report - that complaint comes to us at the national office...it’s easy to pick up facilities that are not monitoring and ordering correctly.
JOHN LINK: Take the fact that vaccinations in this country are voluntary. Mix it with gaps in data collection and widely varying figures from different sources and net result is that we really don’t know who is covered and who isn’t.
Paediatric Public Health Professor Haroon Salojee predicts at least a million children may be at risk. (5 seconds)
PROF. HAROON SALOJEE, PAEDIATRICS AND CHILD HEALTH DEPARTMENT: WITS: In South Africa each year there are about a million births. So if we talk about the 80% measles coverage for example, that means 200 000 children each year...are not being vaccinated. If you take that over five years, that ends up with a million children. And therefore it’s very easy then to have these outbreaks...
In 2015 diphtheria - a deadly vaccine-preventable respiratory infection - resurged in KwaZulu-Natal. (7 seconds)
PROF SHABIR MADHI, DIRECTOR: NATIONAL INSTITUTE FOR COMMUNICABLE DISEASES: Some of the factors relate probably to healthcare services...I think the more important reason is basically complacency on the part of parents... mothers haven’t really identified children dying from measles. It’s something that has happened throughout the world, including in Europe which is experiencing a huge outbreak of measles right now.
Nomazwe Ntsizi and her 8-year-old daughter live with the painful reality of how lethal measles can be. Siyanda, one of twins, was 5 years old when she started having seizures. (10 seconds)
JOHN WEBB: Did they explain to you the role between SSPE and measles?
NOMAZWE NTSIZI, MOM: They explained to me but I was in a state of shock when they explained to me why my child could no longer walk. While they were talking, I could not listen. Because they are twins, one can walk and Siyanda cannot walk.
Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis or SSPE is a rare complication that can develop years after someone contracted measles. It is a progressive and disabling brain condition that will eventually be fatal. (13 seconds)
NOMAZWE NTSIZI, MOM: So I decided to stop working, God would make a plan for me to make ends meet so that I can look after Siyanda because Siyanda needs her medication at a certain time, I can’t miss the time to give her milk. She also needs love because when you have love for a child in her condition, God gives you strength.
Prof Jo Wilmshurst works with these children at the Red Cross Children’s Hospital and saw those with weak immune systems suffer most since the massive 2010 outbreak. In a country with high HIV prevalence and patchy vaccine coverage, complications like SSPE is a real risk. (17 seconds) (http://www.samj.org.za/index.php/samj/article/view/5984/4424)
(http://www.who.int/mediacentre/factsheets/fs286/en/)
PROF. JO WILMSHURST, PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGIST: RED CROSS MEMORIAL CHILDREN’S HOSPITAL: The crisis that happened in 2010/2011 was a world-wide crisis and the hardest group hit were infants. Where families elect not to vaccinate their children, where the programs aren’t sufficiently set out, so there’s no access to vaccine programs and where the child can’t actually respond or take up the vaccine appropriately and in those situations you then start getting children who are at risk.
In some cases the system fails kids -- in others, people choose not to vaccinate. One reason is the lingering effects of a now debunked and discredited paper published in the respected Lancet journal in 1998 that had suggested a link between autism and vaccines. (16 seconds)
PROF. JO WILMSHURST, PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGIST: RED CROSS MEMORIAL CHILDREN’S HOSPITAL: This caused horror and fear and concern. The tragedy is that when they actually looked at the way the study was done and the children that were affected and this was being intensely interrogated. There was absolutely no evidence whatsoever linking that the measles vaccine had caused the autism.
In 2010 the Lancet withdrew the article. (3 seconds)
PROF. HAROON SALOJEE, PAEDIATRICS AND CHILD HEALTH DEPARTMENT: WITS: The current measles outbreak is actually a group of Muslim parents in Lenasia who have again chosen not to, for religious reasons including for example that some, some vaccines contained gelatine, animal gelatine and they say it’s not Halaal and not Kosher. These arguments don’t hold any water...the religious authorities have said very clearly, give vaccinations to your children. They save lives.
A national catch-up campaign was run in June, but for the Department of Health, every day is immunisation day. (6 seconds)
JOHN WEBB: Should we be concerned about the outbreaks at Johannesburg and Cape Town?
PROF. GREG HUSSEY, DIRECTOR: VACCINES FOR AFRICA: I think the important thing is to ensure that your children receive two doses of measles vaccine. And I mean, I think That’s the bottom line. One of the problems with our immunisation program is the fact that we don’t have good advocacy and communication strategy.
NTOMBI MAZIBUKO, DIRECTOR: CHILD, YOUTH AND SCHOOL HEALTH, DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH: We need to make sure that all the services are integrated -- if a child comes for anything else, the healthcare worker says I am going to offer you vaccination today.
PROMOS:
10 secs
Measles outbreaks have flared up here and across the world, severely affecting thousands. Should South Africa revisit its free but voluntary childhood vaccination program?

15 secs
More than 80 South Africans have had measles so far this year but this could be just the beginning.
PROF SHABIR MADHI: If we’re not careful this figure … is going to be exactly what it was in 2009/2010 and that is going to 20 000 as a conservative estimate.

15 secs
Immunisation is free but voluntary -- what does that mean for the health of the broader community?
PROF JO WILMSHURST: With the herd immunity that’s been in place with regular immune programs, you kind of forget about the era when measles was an issue.

Further information: STOCKOUT: VACCINES THAT DON’T ARRIVE 21 FEBRUARY, 2017 EUROSCIENTIST Everyone agrees that these shortages are a global problem, due to the fact that the vaccines are developed by just a handful of companies, those with the sufficient human and financial capacity. If one of these companies has production problems, countries have few alternatives to satisfy demand. In cases of high demand, the market becomes saturated and the companies are unable to satisfy demand to all countries. Whilst certain, this excuse restricts liability to uncontrollable, external, factors. Internal factors are not curbed and are only reported by healthcare staff. On a global level, according to World Health Organization data (WHO), 97 countries accounted for that they were left without at least one of the essential vaccines in 2015 (the last year for which data is available) either on a national level on in certain areas. In Africa, 66% of countries acknowledged supply disruption. In America and Europe one in every two countries admitted having suffered this problem. Taking into account the fact that not all countries communicate this information to the WHO, the real number of countries without vaccines at any moment could be greater still. Out of stock against tuberculosis. The anti-tuberculosis BCG vaccine is a prime case of a supply problem, caused by a production failures in one of the main labs of this vaccine, Statens Serum Institute, based in Denmark. Due to global shortages in 2015, 54 countries reported stock shortages this year. The majority of these countries are in Africa (21) and Europe (14). In 2015, UNICEF, who supply this vaccine to countries where tuberculosis is endemic, reported a global supply shortage of 16.5 million doses. Beyond the crisis that year, many countries have been lacking the BCG vaccine for over a decade. Stockouts of anti tuberculosis vaccine. Number of years in the last decade which stockouts reported to the WHO in the last decade. Currently, stock problems with the tuberculosis vaccine persist, including in countries that had never previously reported a shortage of the antigen to the WHO, such as Spain, Australia and France. In the case of France, where the vaccine is no longer obligatory since 2007, Sanofi Pasteur (the French pharmaceutical company specialised in vaccines) diverted its stock which was destined for the Polish market in order to satisfy domestic demand. This diversion was introduced as an “interim measure” in March 2016. In South Africa, this vaccine is especially relevant and its shortage is “a real problem”, according to Doctor Anban Pillay, Deputy Director of the Department of Health. Although its effectiveness is limited against pulmonary tuberculosis, its most common manifestation, the WHO recommends its administration to new born babies in countries where the incidence (morbility) of tuberculosis is high. In South Africa, morbility is huge: with 834 cases for every 100,000 people, the country has the highest rates of this disease, often compounded by the impact of HIV. The BCG vaccine supply crisis is worsened by the concentration of production in few companies. And low profit margins makes it an unattractive venture for other laboratories which have the capacity to produce it, appoints Pillay. The oligopoly of the vaccines industry is even more concentrated: Sanofi Pasteur, Merck, Pfizer and GlaxoSmithKline take around 80% of the proceeds globally from the sales of these products. Bexsero stockout in the EU - Bexsero, the only vaccine available in the European Union which protects against Meningitis B, the most common serogroup in the continent, is currently suffering distribution problems. The antigen, produced by GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) is approved in over 35 countries, between which are the EU member states, Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Canada, Brazil and the USA. This last country also depends on another drug for the disease, Trumemba. In Spain, where the vaccine is recommended but unsubsidised, pharmacies offer waiting lists of up to six months to obtain a dose (at a retail price of 105€). GSK Spain asserts that they will receive new doses in the second quarter of 2017. Other GSK subsidiaries have also reported problems with the manufacture of this vaccine, like in Australia and in the United Kingdom, due to “unanticipated global demand”. Lack of control in South Africa - In South Africa, provinces that default on their payments for vaccines are another of the missing links in the supply chain, according to Shabir Madhi, director of the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD). The South African government negotiates the prices and Biovac, a public-private partnership, receive the raw materials from the pharmacists. In their premises in Ciudad del Cabo, they fill vials and distribute the orders that they receive from provinces. Both Madhi and Pillay claim that Biovac has frozen supply to certain provinces which have not paid. Once the vaccines have been distributed to the South African clinics the stock management problems begin to arise. Karl le Roux, doctor and researcher from Zithuele hospital, analysed the causes and effects of vaccines stockouts in the OR Tambo district, in the Eastern Cape province. According to his research, the shortages are due to a lack of space in the clinics, inadequate stock management systems, overworked staff and poorly trained nurses (that make orders for inadequate quantities), lack of responsibility in the provincial storage and theft. Moreover, the state of the roads and the distance from storage facilities to healthcare centres are even more important in rural areas. Le Roux tells, for example, that there are 90 kilometres of very poor roads between Zithuele hospital and its medicine depot. For this rural doctor “it is frustrating not being able to offer a patient what you know they need”. As soon as there is a shortage of vaccines, the centres are swamped as patients have to return. In his research, Karl le Roux shows that the lack of vaccines in clinics meant that 56% of children surveyed did not complete their courses of immunisation, according to their mothers. Unreliable data - Johann Van der Heever, who managed the South African immunization programme for 11 years, blames the lack of control squarely on the Department of Health: “You have to staff adequately to the chain, you have to provide equip supervision and monitoring which is a function of the National Department”. In an article in the South African Medical Journal magazine, which cites Van der Heever’s criticisms of the national immunization programme and condemns the government’s neglect of the situation, the national cold-chain manager (imperative system for the conservation of the antigens), admits that they were only able to inspect between 5% and 10% of facilities. Van der Heever regrets that, despite the fact that controlling the deterioration of vaccines was one of his priorities, the wastage is unknown, as it “requires very good supervision and support”. “One of the big problems that we have is manufacturers have been aware that they have a shortage but they have not been willing to share that information, unlike in the United States or in Europe, where they are obliged by law”, alleged the Deputy Director of the Department of Health, Anban Pillay. Given the time required to produce each vaccine, both internal and external information is imperative in order to avoid stockouts. “You can only be foresighted if you have the information”, stated the healthcare manager. The only way to approach to the real situation is through the Stop Stockouts Project (SSP), a platform that monitors the lack of medicines and vaccines in South Africa. Behind the project are organisations such as Médecins Sans Frontières, the Treatment Action Campaign and the Rural Health Advocacy Project, which created the campaign in light of the persistent lack of antiretroviral drugs in the country which has the highest number of HIV cases in the world (over 6.9 million people): one in five adults is seropositive. At the end of each year, SSP conducts a telephone interview about vaccines and stockouts with over 2,400 of the 3,547 healthcare centres that they have identified across the country. Whilst Jacob Zuma’s government only reported its stock issues with the BCG vaccine to the WHO in 2015, Stop Stockouts recorded that 9% of healthcare centres contacted did not have the combined vaccine (composed of the DPT vaccine and the vaccines against Polio, Hib and Hepatitis B) available; 4% did not have the rotavirus vaccine available and 3% had a shortage of measles vaccines. The data is indispensable: to control the existence of vaccines in stores, to know when to make an efficient order for a clinic and to design effective vaccination campaigns that avoid possible outbreaks in communities with low immunisation rates. Coordinated administration and the shouldering of responsibilities is vital to avoid shortages and stockouts of vaccines nationwide. But above all, South Africa cannot allow its people to lose faith in its healthcare system. South Africa: managing in the dark - Problems with data in South Africa do not only affect stock levels; the most basic data, such as immunization rates, are not reliable. The lack of an up-to-date and detailed survey on vaccination coverage makes it impossible to control and avoid possible outbreaks, according to Shabir Madhi of the National Institute of Contagious Diseases in South Africa, as it is not known in which areas immunization is lower than recommended. “We do not know the actual coverage against measles,” laments Madhi. In addition, the WHO reduces by more than 20 points the levels of coverage that South Africa presents to them. Madhi, who estimates that the real figure must be between both values, urges to carry out a new survey to solve this situation. Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 23 July 2017 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 01 August 2017 Press Release: Outbreak First in Cape Town and now in Gauteng – scientists have confirmed over a hundred cases of highly contagious measles. South Africa’s voluntary childhood vaccination programme was intended to prevent the mass outbreak of disease, but these cases are an indication that the system may be flawed. Are there cracks in the country’s vaccination plans? Script: SCRIPT: Outbreak TX DATE: TBC PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg PRESENTER: John Webb The plan was to eliminate measles worldwide by 2020. But outbreaks are flaring up -- 6 600 cases in Romania; 2 800 in Italy; and in Minnesota, USA, 78 since April. Most had not been vaccinated against measles and one sick person can infect up to 15 others. In South Africa 83 cases were confirmed up to mid-June. One of the first was 17-year-old Neels Neethling from Paul Roos Gimnasium in Stellenbosch. (31 seconds) References for numbers: Romania, Italy: http://ecdc.europa.eu/en/press/news/_layouts/forms/News_DispForm.aspx?ID=1631&List=8db7286c-fe2d-476c-9133-18ff4cb1b568&Source=http%3A%2F%2Fecdc%2Eeuropa%2Eeu%2Fen%2Fpress%2Fepidemiological_updates%2FPages%2Fepidemiological_updates%2Easpx / Minnesota: http://www.health.state.mn.us/divs/idepc/diseases/measles/#1 NEELS NEETHLING, MATRIC PUPIL: PAUL ROOS GIMNASIUM: My roommate said to me I must go away so that he doesn’t contract it, because it spreads quickly. His mom, GP Amanda Neethling, was first to spot the telltale rash and made sure Neels got treatment quickly. (7 seconds) AMANDA NEETHLING, MOM AND GENERAL PRACTITIONER: Within hours, your child just gets more ill and you get really nervous. I was also afraid, you know, there is a chance of a secondary infection. And then the fact that you know your child was immunised and you don’t quite understand why the child contracted it. Paul Roos Gimnasium was on high alert. They considered it their legal and ethical duty to go to lock-down. Spokesman Neville Rothman. (8 seconds) NEVILLE ROTHMAN, COMMUNICATION MANAGER: PAUL ROOS GIMNASIUM: Between Paul Roos, Bloemhof Girl’s School and Renish Girl’s School we had a collective meeting with the experts and they told us that containment was the most important...but they encouraged us to almost not get involved with other sporting activities...we do not want to be seen as compromising other people. In the end, 7 pupils contracted measles. There’ve been 29 cases in the Western Cape. Before vaccines, millions - mostly kids under 5 - died of measles and thousands developed complications like blindness and pneumonia annually. Vaccines also prevent other deadly diseases like polio and diphtheria. (18 seconds) (source: http://www.nicd.ac.za/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/MeaslesGautengAlertJune2017.pdfhttp://www.nicd.ac.za/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/MeaslesGautengAlertJune2017.pdf) (http://apps.who.int/iris/bitstream/10665/44855/1/9789241503396_eng.pdf) (http://www.who.int/mediacentre/factsheets/fs286/en/) JOHN LINK: Whenever cases of measles, diphtheria or meningitis in particular are identified, they tend to be referred to as outbreaks, but is that the result of an exaggeration by government or a valid reason for concern? Prof Shabir Madhi, award-winning vaccine scientist who played a key role in developing the rotavirus and pneumococcal vaccines, heads the government-funded National Institute for Communicable Diseases that must confirm whether a sore throat and runny nose means measles. (16 seconds) PROF. SHABIR MADHI, DIRECTOR: NATIONAL INSTITUTE FOR COMMUNICABLE DISEASES: When we see this sort of measles outbreaks, it’s a good indicator in terms of how well our immunisation program is working and the reason for that is unlike for many of the other diseases that we’ve vaccinate against, measles is the most contagious of all of them. Last month, 17 cases were confirmed in Gauteng. Now, Azaadville on the West Rand is the hot spot, with 8 cases so far, mostly adults. (9 seconds) PROF. SHABIR MADHI, DIRECTOR: NATIONAL INSTITUTE FOR COMMUNICABLE DISEASES: Right now we’re not actually at the peak of this epidemic. Right? If we’re not careful this figure of roughly about 85 cases that we’ve observed in Gauteng in the past two or three months, is going to be exactly what it was in 2009/2010 and that is going to 20 000 as a conservative estimate. And that’s when we see many more children dying. Right? So right now, this is… we’re sort of still brewing an epidemic. Our Expanded Programme on Immunisation -- or EPI -- is run by the health department under the guidance of the World Health Organisation. Eleven vaccines are given without cost at clinics, but not every child gets it/them?. (13 seconds) (source: http://www.afro.who.int/en/south-africa/country-programmes/4245-expanded-program-on-immunization-epi.html) JOHN LINK: A successful immunisation program could lead to healthier children and adults in the long run and help ease the burden on the public health system, but ironically the country’s vaccination program appears to become another victim of that self-same overburdened and understaffed system. Prof Greg Hussey runs the National Advisory Group on Immunisation that works with the Minister and Department of Health to find and fix problems in the system. (9 seconds) PROF. GREG HUSSEY, DIRECTOR: VACCINES FOR AFRICA: Our supply chain is not functioning optimally. Stockouts occur because of poor stock management firstly and secondly supply. The Minister in his budget speech alluded to the fact that they’re trying to rectify that. They now have electronic system to monitor stocks of all medication in clinics and hospitals. We’ve had major issues globally with supply of vaccines. To begin to eliminate measles at least 95% of children must get both prescribed doses -- at 6 and 12 months old. (8 seconds) NTOMBI MAZIBUKO, DIRECTOR: CHILD, YOUTH AND SCHOOL HEALTH, DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH: The health system as a whole there are quite a lot of challenges...it looks like an easy programme but the important thing is that caregivers, parents must still take their children to a health facility. At the National Department of Health, Ntombi Mazibuko works on innovations in the hope it will get more kids covered. (6 seconds) NTOMBI MAZIBUKO, DIRECTOR: CHILD, YOUTH AND SCHOOL HEALTH, DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH: We are now looking at making sure that people are empowered -- otherwise why will they go to the clinic and stand in the queue the whole day, for my child is not sick... The Minister launched what we call MOMCONNECT -- a service where mothers register when they’re pregnant. The SMS service, which works on any phone, is meant to remind moms of vaccination dates...and to report problems at clinics. (7 seconds) NTOMBI MAZIBUKO, DIRECTOR: CHILD, YOUTH AND SCHOOL HEALTH, DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH: The mothers can also through the MOMCONNECT report - that complaint comes to us at the national office...it’s easy to pick up facilities that are not monitoring and ordering correctly. JOHN LINK: Take the fact that vaccinations in this country are voluntary. Mix it with gaps in data collection and widely varying figures from different sources and net result is that we really don’t know who is covered and who isn’t. Paediatric Public Health Professor Haroon Salojee predicts at least a million children may be at risk. (5 seconds) PROF. HAROON SALOJEE, PAEDIATRICS AND CHILD HEALTH DEPARTMENT: WITS: In South Africa each year there are about a million births. So if we talk about the 80% measles coverage for example, that means 200 000 children each year...are not being vaccinated. If you take that over five years, that ends up with a million children. And therefore it’s very easy then to have these outbreaks... In 2015 diphtheria - a deadly vaccine-preventable respiratory infection - resurged in KwaZulu-Natal. (7 seconds) PROF SHABIR MADHI, DIRECTOR: NATIONAL INSTITUTE FOR COMMUNICABLE DISEASES: Some of the factors relate probably to healthcare services...I think the more important reason is basically complacency on the part of parents... mothers haven’t really identified children dying from measles. It’s something that has happened throughout the world, including in Europe which is experiencing a huge outbreak of measles right now. Nomazwe Ntsizi and her 8-year-old daughter live with the painful reality of how lethal measles can be. Siyanda, one of twins, was 5 years old when she started having seizures. (10 seconds) JOHN WEBB: Did they explain to you the role between SSPE and measles? NOMAZWE NTSIZI, MOM: They explained to me but I was in a state of shock when they explained to me why my child could no longer walk. While they were talking, I could not listen. Because they are twins, one can walk and Siyanda cannot walk. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis or SSPE is a rare complication that can develop years after someone contracted measles. It is a progressive and disabling brain condition that will eventually be fatal. (13 seconds) NOMAZWE NTSIZI, MOM: So I decided to stop working, God would make a plan for me to make ends meet so that I can look after Siyanda because Siyanda needs her medication at a certain time, I can’t miss the time to give her milk. She also needs love because when you have love for a child in her condition, God gives you strength. Prof Jo Wilmshurst works with these children at the Red Cross Children’s Hospital and saw those with weak immune systems suffer most since the massive 2010 outbreak. In a country with high HIV prevalence and patchy vaccine coverage, complications like SSPE is a real risk. (17 seconds) (http://www.samj.org.za/index.php/samj/article/view/5984/4424) (http://www.who.int/mediacentre/factsheets/fs286/en/) PROF. JO WILMSHURST, PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGIST: RED CROSS MEMORIAL CHILDREN’S HOSPITAL: The crisis that happened in 2010/2011 was a world-wide crisis and the hardest group hit were infants. Where families elect not to vaccinate their children, where the programs aren’t sufficiently set out, so there’s no access to vaccine programs and where the child can’t actually respond or take up the vaccine appropriately and in those situations you then start getting children who are at risk. In some cases the system fails kids -- in others, people choose not to vaccinate. One reason is the lingering effects of a now debunked and discredited paper published in the respected Lancet journal in 1998 that had suggested a link between autism and vaccines. (16 seconds) PROF. JO WILMSHURST, PAEDIATRIC NEUROLOGIST: RED CROSS MEMORIAL CHILDREN’S HOSPITAL: This caused horror and fear and concern. The tragedy is that when they actually looked at the way the study was done and the children that were affected and this was being intensely interrogated. There was absolutely no evidence whatsoever linking that the measles vaccine had caused the autism. In 2010 the Lancet withdrew the article. (3 seconds) PROF. HAROON SALOJEE, PAEDIATRICS AND CHILD HEALTH DEPARTMENT: WITS: The current measles outbreak is actually a group of Muslim parents in Lenasia who have again chosen not to, for religious reasons including for example that some, some vaccines contained gelatine, animal gelatine and they say it’s not Halaal and not Kosher. These arguments don’t hold any water...the religious authorities have said very clearly, give vaccinations to your children. They save lives. A national catch-up campaign was run in June, but for the Department of Health, every day is immunisation day. (6 seconds) JOHN WEBB: Should we be concerned about the outbreaks at Johannesburg and Cape Town? PROF. GREG HUSSEY, DIRECTOR: VACCINES FOR AFRICA: I think the important thing is to ensure that your children receive two doses of measles vaccine. And I mean, I think That’s the bottom line. One of the problems with our immunisation program is the fact that we don’t have good advocacy and communication strategy. NTOMBI MAZIBUKO, DIRECTOR: CHILD, YOUTH AND SCHOOL HEALTH, DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH: We need to make sure that all the services are integrated -- if a child comes for anything else, the healthcare worker says I am going to offer you vaccination today. PROMOS: 10 secs Measles outbreaks have flared up here and across the world, severely affecting thousands. Should South Africa revisit its free but voluntary childhood vaccination program? 15 secs More than 80 South Africans have had measles so far this year but this could be just the beginning. PROF SHABIR MADHI: If we’re not careful this figure … is going to be exactly what it was in 2009/2010 and that is going to 20 000 as a conservative estimate. 15 secs Immunisation is free but voluntary -- what does that mean for the health of the broader community? PROF JO WILMSHURST: With the herd immunity that’s been in place with regular immune programs, you kind of forget about the era when measles was an issue.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): 17 cases of measles are confirmed in Gauteng, linked to a family who chose not to immunise their children. We analyse cracks in the country's voluntary vaccination programme that put us all at risk.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: When Johann van den Heever, manager of South Africa's Extended Immunisation programme for 11 years resigned in protest over cracks in the programme early last year, the Department of Health slated him for speaking out about problems that he had said would make all South Africans vulnerable for diseases that should and could have been eradicated by now. The departing manager was interviewed by Science Writer Chris Bateman who published the interview in the South African Medical Journal that showed how severe understaffing, vaccine stock-outs and poor follow-up was causing children not to get the full complement of shots they should. Bateman will speak to us about the facts uncovered by his story a year ago -- the former manager was lambasted and runs scared of speaking out again. South Africa makes 11 antigens available in the extended immunisation schedule -- from measles, to the most recent HPV vaccine for protecting young girls agains caner of the cervix. Thanks to vaccines, polio and diptheria and whooping cough have been eliminated. But aside from measles, Kwazulu-Natal saw a resurgence of diptheria two years ago. Through outbreak data and case studies we can basically track and confirm problems in the system as one outbreak after another hits the headlines -- there have now been three measles outbreaks (from over 31 confirmed cases in Stellenbosch to JHB) before the winter season, traditionally outbreak season, has even started. Bateman warned in his article that missed vaccine doses were causing our herd immunity to be diminished, which would open doors to infections that could and should have been prevented. Add to this the growing, if misguided fear that vaccines cause illness and autism in children, and the country's promise to the world community that we would eradicate measles by 2020, after the WHO DECADE OF VACCINES, seems highly improbable. A massive educational responsibility rests on media in covering the outbreak -- the Lancet publication in 1998 by scientist Andrew Wakefield that linked the measles, mumps and vaccine to autism has been withdrawn, and described by Lancet as unethical, dishonest and fatally flawed. And yet this thinking continues to feed fears around autism. The minister of health recently said members of the anti-vax lobby (resperented by VASA, Vaccine Awareness SA) are no better than bio-terrorists for placing everyone at risk by eroding the good work done by the department over many years. But it's not just those who CHOOSE not to vaccinate that cause the problem -- it's also those who forget, because their babies look well...and other migrants that fall out of the system, for a variety of logistical reasons -- shown in WHO studies in SA that we will review.
metadata.Summary: Our proposal is to start with BATEMAN, to show the cracks in the immunisation programme -- then to look at the outbreak map that the National Institute of Communicable Diseases keeps (any instance of 3 laboratory-confirmed cases constitutes an outbreak). We will tell of 2 TYPES OF PATIENTS/CASE STUDIES who fall through the cracks -- the anti-vax child whose parents object for factual or religious beliefs; as well as the child who misses a dose due to vaccine stockouts, poor follow-up or unavailability of staff. We will show the history of some of the most dangerous illnesses successfully eradicated through vaccines and show the science "fixed" by Lancet after the damaging publication of the WAKEFIELD study in 1998. Turns out he wasn't interested in eradicating vaccines...but in replacing the vaccine in use with his own invention.

Le Roux tells, for example, that there are 90 kilometres of very poor roads between Zithuele hospital and its medicine depot. For this rural doctor “it is frustrating not being able to offer a patient what you know they need”. As soon as there is a shortage of vaccines, the centres are swamped as patients have to return. In his research, Karl le Roux shows that the lack of vaccines in clinics meant that 56% of children surveyed did not complete their courses of immunisation, according to their mothers. Unreliable data - Johann Van der Heever, who managed the South African immunization programme for 11 years, blames the lack of control squarely on the Department of Health: “You have to staff adequately to the chain, you have to provide equip supervision and monitoring which is a function of the National Department”. In an article in the South African Medical Journal magazine, which cites Van der Heever’s criticisms of the national immunization programme and condemns the government’s neglect of the situation, the national cold-chain manager (imperative system for the conservation of the antigens), admits that they were only able to inspect between 5% and 10% of facilities. Van der Heever regrets that, despite the fact that controlling the deterioration of vaccines was one of his priorities, the wastage is unknown, as it “requires very good supervision and support”. “One of the big problems that we have is manufacturers have been aware that they have a shortage but they have not been willing to share that information, unlike in the United States or in Europe, where they are obliged by law”, alleged the Deputy Director of the Department of Health, Anban Pillay. Given the time required to produce each vaccine, both internal and external information is imperative in order to avoid stockouts. “You can only be foresighted if you have the information”, stated the healthcare manager. The only way to approach to the real situation is through the Stop Stockouts Project (SSP), a platform that monitors the lack of medicines and vaccines in South Africa. Behind the project are organisations such as Médecins Sans Frontières, the Treatment Action Campaign and the Rural Health Advocacy Project, which created the campaign in light of the persistent lack of antiretroviral drugs in the country which has the highest number of HIV cases in the world (over 6.9 million people): one in five adults is seropositive. At the end of each year, SSP conducts a telephone interview about vaccines and stockouts with over 2,400 of the 3,547 healthcare centres that they have identified across the country. Whilst Jacob Zuma’s government only reported its stock issues with the BCG vaccine to the WHO in 2015, Stop Stockouts recorded that 9% of healthcare centres contacted did not have the combined vaccine (composed of the DPT vaccine and the vaccines against Polio, Hib and Hepatitis B) available; 4% did not have the rotavirus vaccine available and 3% had a shortage of measles vaccines. The data is indispensable: to control the existence of vaccines in stores, to know when to make an efficient order for a clinic and to design effective vaccination campaigns that avoid possible outbreaks in communities with low immunisation rates. Coordinated administration and the shouldering of responsibilities is vital to avoid shortages and stockouts of vaccines nationwide. But above all, South Africa cannot allow its people to lose faith in its healthcare system. South Africa: managing in the dark - Problems with data in South Africa do not only affect stock levels; the most basic data, such as immunization rates, are not reliable. The lack of an up-to-date and detailed survey on vaccination coverage makes it impossible to control and avoid possible outbreaks, according to Shabir Madhi of the National Institute of Contagious Diseases in South Africa, as it is not known in which areas immunization is lower than recommended. “We do not know the actual coverage against measles,” laments Madhi. In addition, the WHO reduces by more than 20 points the levels of coverage that South Africa presents to them. Madhi, who estimates that the real figure must be between both values, urges to carry out a new survey to solve this situation.
